item.title: Each building tells a story: A New York City neighborhood on the cusp of densification
item.description:
Mara Sidney, Tamara Velasquez Leiferman, Joshua McWhirter
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261500283
This study seeks to understand the business of densification through analysis of public policies, property records, and “the everyday” in a rapidly changing Manhattan neighborhood. Our case study of Inwood uses a new conceptual framework for urban policy analysis to bring multiple data sources together to examine four sites that show how key elements of New York City’s rezoning strategy intersects with other housing policies. Our findings speak to the challenges of maintaining affordable housing stock amid densification and the importance of including everyday experiences in policy analysis. We find that new densification policies interact with pre-existing policies to produce complex, contradictory outcomes. For example, de-densification coexists with densification. Second, although some manifestations of densification are visible, such as high-rise buildings, others are not, including tenant displacement and apartment warehousing. Finally, we find that policy implementation works as ad hoc policy making because actors seek policy changes through alternative channels after rezoning is formally adopted.

item.title: The rubble and beyond: Expanding urbicide through affective geographies and the settler-colonial longue durée
item.description:
Ohoud Kamal, Yamen N. Al-Betawi
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261503755
Urbicide scholarship has established, in varying ways, that ‘killing a city’ reaches beyond the material. Yet the concepts used to name this ‘reach’ do not describe the same object or make the same analytical claim. The question is therefore not only whether urbicide reaches beyond the material, but what a given conceptualisation allows us to understand about what destruction reaches. This article expands urbicide scholarship by theorising affect not as an additional dimension or effect of destruction, but as a capacity enabled by material and human–nonhuman relations through which violence can be reached. The argument is developed through a situated reading of contemporary urbicidal violence in Gaza (2023–ongoing), where recurrent military operations have compounded destruction while foreclosing reconstruction between them, within a longer settler-colonial history of displacement and enclosure. Drawing on Anderson’s account of morale and affective geographies literature, the article shows how destruction reaches the material and relational conditions through which affective capacities are constituted and exercised. It further proposes storytelling and counter-mapping as situated forms of evidence for tracing the reach of this destruction: memories, attachments, spatial knowledge and relations that conventional damage assessment cannot capture. Locating these processes within the settler-colonial longue durée expands the concept of urbicide showing how its reach is shaped by historically specific conditions of enclosure, cumulative destruction and the absence of a stable aftermath.
